opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to separate what you can control from what you can't. When you're building something like Kimi, there are going to be moments when everything seems to be going right: the product gets attention, users are growing, the model hits a new capability. And there are moments when a competitor releases something strong, or the numbers don't move the way you hoped, or the market narrative suddenly turns against you. If your emotional state follows those external signals, you'll be exhausted very quickly.

So for me, I try to anchor on a few things that don't change much day to day. The first is the technical conviction: why we believe this direction matters, why scaling intelligence is worth pursuing, and what we think the path to better models looks like. That belief doesn't depend on a single week's metrics. If the reasoning still holds, then a bad week is just noise, and a good week is also just noise.

The second is to think in longer time horizons. AGI, or whatever you want to call it, is not a sprint that ends next quarter. It's a very long process, probably over many years. When you zoom out, many of the highs and lows that feel huge in the moment become small fluctuations on a longer curve. That perspective helps me stay calm and not overreact.

The third is to focus on the work itself. In the end, what really matters is whether the model gets better, whether the team keeps learning, and whether we're solving real problems for users. When I'm anxious, the best remedy is usually to go back to the concrete problems: look at the data, look at the training runs, talk with the researchers. Doing the actual work is grounding.

And honestly, I think a bit of humility helps too. You have to accept that there's a lot of uncertainty, and you will make mistakes. Instead of treating each setback as a crisis, you treat it as information. What did we get wrong? What can we learn? If you can keep that learning attitude, then the lows become part of the process rather than something that breaks you.

So it's not that I don't feel the ups and downs. Of course I do. But I try not to let them define the direction. The direction comes from what we believe is right in the long run.

r001.rationale: The response says to focus on the work itself and return to concrete problems, explaining that doing the actual work is grounding when anxious.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the most important thing is to not tie your sense of self too tightly to whatever the market is saying about you in any given week. When we started Moonshot, there was a period where everyone was very excited, and then there were periods where people wrote us off. If you let that drive your emotional state, you're going to be exhausted very quickly, because the external narrative swings far more than the actual underlying work does.

What I try to come back to is: are we making progress on the things we believe matter? For us that's always been scaling, long context, reasoning, agents, and building a model that people actually find useful. Those questions have fairly objective answers. The loss curve doesn't care whether we're trending. If the research is moving forward and the team is learning, then the week is a good week, even if the headlines are bad. And if the research isn't moving, no amount of good press should make me feel comfortable.

The second thing is time horizon. I genuinely believe AGI is one of the most important technological transitions in history, and the path there is going to be long and nonlinear. If you look at a ten- or twenty-year window, most of the ups and downs we're talking about are noise. That framing isn't just a coping mechanism, it's also strategically correct. A lot of mistakes in this field come from people optimizing for how they look over the next three months.

And the last thing, which I've learned the hard way, is that the lows are usually more informative than the highs. When something goes wrong, when a release underperforms, when a competitor ships something that makes you rethink your roadmap, that's when you learn fastest. I try to treat those moments as data rather than as a verdict on whether we deserve to exist. If you can hold that mindset, the lows become almost useful, and the highs you just enjoy for a day and then get back to work.

r001.rationale: The response says to focus on progress in the work that matters—such as research moving forward and the team learning—rather than market reactions, as a way to handle highs and lows.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to keep your attention on the work itself. When things are going well, it’s easy to feel that every decision you made was right. When things are difficult, it’s easy to question everything. Neither is a very useful way to judge progress.

For me, a more useful question is: Are we learning? Are we getting closer to understanding what makes the model better and what users actually need? Those questions give you something concrete to focus on, even when the outcome is uncertain.

That doesn’t mean you don’t feel the highs and lows. But you can try to avoid letting them determine your next decision. Keep the long-term direction steady, and be willing to change how you get there.

r001.rationale: The response says to keep attention on the work itself and focus on learning and improving the model, presenting this as a way to stay steady through highs and lows.

sol-6.1.text:
I try to focus on whether we’re learning and making real progress, rather than letting each result determine my mood. When things go well, it’s easy to think you’ve figured everything out. When things go badly, it’s easy to question the whole direction. Neither reaction is necessarily useful.

For me, the way to stay grounded is to come back to concrete questions: What did we learn? What’s the most important problem now? What can we try next? You can’t control every outcome, but you can keep improving the quality of your decisions.

And you need some distance from the work, too. If your perspective becomes one experiment or one product release, every fluctuation feels enormous. Taking a longer view helps you stay ambitious without being consumed by the ups and downs.

r001.rationale: The response says to focus on learning, progress, and improving decision quality rather than letting outcomes dictate mood, presenting attention to the work itself as a way to stay grounded through ups and downs.
